We programmers often talk about the importance of clean code. I have talked many times about the topic, for example <a href="https://www.joantolos.com/blog/readability" target="_blank">here</a> or <a href="https://www.joantolos.com/blog/java-encapsulation" target="_blank">here</a>. I don't want to talk about what clean code is and what it isn't, but how embracing the right attitude, this "clean way" of performing your job, can easily transpose to other aspects of your life.

# Once upon a time...

I was not always so lucky to have this job where I type words on a keyboard for a living. Like many of you, I navigated through various jobs during my teenage years to fund my university education. Raised in a modest household with a strict work ethic, I observed my father, a construction worker like his father before him, exemplify the value of hard work. Education wasn't my father's forte, and my grandfather's approach to schooling was straightforward: _"If you don't want to attend school, you'll work alongside me"_. With that, my father became a construction worker, closing the chapter on academic pursuits.

He learned the trade alongside his father and made a living with his hands and back. Later on, he specialized as a plasterer, which gave him the opportunity to build decorative pieces that were going to the ceilings of some prestigious buildings in the city. Some of his work was very artistic and beautiful, creating pieces with symmetrical forms and rich patterns. This lateral move also allowed him to work more in the workshop and not so much in the field, which was the correct move as he aged.

My father's version of that ultimatum for me was way better: _"You are old enough to start making some money, so you are coming with me to learn how to do that. **You don't have to do what I do, but you have to do something**"_. Which I think is a pretty good improvement from the previous generation. 

So there I went, waking up really early in the morning to work in construction during my school summer vacation.

# The days of building stuff with my hands

I remember my first day joining the crew of workers, attending a bustling meeting where tasks were swiftly delegated for the weeks ahead. I can say it was maybe my fisrt job meeting: an informal gathering characterized by urgency and efficiency. Naturally, I wasn't paired with my father, a partnership that would've seemed too convenient, perhaps "working with daddy". Instead, I suspect my father arranged for me to be paired with some decent guy, but not himself.

So, after a few words, everyone went to their respective cars for commuting to their particular jobs. I sat in the car with my new partner named Santi and I was genuinely terrified. My father went one way, I went another.

This guy was quite the character, a compact and intense figure, like a coiled wire. Stoic, silent, and strong, he possessed a demeanor that commanded respect. Never used two words when only one was required. Severe but fair.

As we grew accustomed to each other over the days, our dynamic evolved. I found myself entrusted with more engaging tasks beyond the routine chores of sweeping, cleaning and organizing. By the end of our time together, we had truly become partners in our work. While he handled the intricate skilled tasks, I took the initiative to manage my time effectively, contributing more to the job. 
I could be on top of a ladder plastering some ceiling and he was sweeping the floor. The roles were clear, yet he always treated me with the respect of a colleague. I like to believe that I earned his respect through my willingness to learn.

From time to time, the big boss appeared on our job site and just walked around, observing stuff. Again, not many words were exchanged. He had an aura of _wise man_ and everyone seemed to respect and value him a lot. One thing that he did was just looking at the floor in the particular place we were working. If we were working on some arrangements on top of a column, adding some decorative piece to make the column better blend with the ceiling, he was always looking... at the floor! Not just looking but inspecting, like we actually did some work on the floor, which we didn't.

I was genuinely curious. Why was this man looking at the floor when the progress was happening on the ceiling? I asked my father, and he told me to ask him myself.

The days passed and I finally gathered the courage to ask him the question on the very last day of the job, when the whole crew was gathered again... "Why do you always look at the floor when you come visit?" and he simply answered: “Because how you do one thing, you do them all". Then he just walked away. I looked at my father, and he looked at me with an expression saying: “there you go, you have your answer". And that was the end of it.

To make the story short, I went to work with them a couple more times and finally switched to a desktop job, less physically demanding (and infinitely more boring). I finished my studies, got my first job as a programmer, and the rest is history. It was fairly recently when I realized how similar our jobs really are. We both use our creativity and tools available to build a small part of a bigger system. We want to do a quality job and be proud of the result while remaining within a budget and a timeline. We need our job to be easy to maintain and grow. 

When I try to explain those similarities to him, he doesn't quite get it but sometimes I smile thinking that maybe I ended up following my father's steps after all. My grandfather would be weirdly proud (and confused).

I learned two lessons from this whole experience:

- I am able to do this job.
- I don't want to do this job.

Pretty good insights for a teenager. Don't get me wrong, it is a very nice way to make a living, it's just not my thing.

# How you do one thing is how you do them all

I took the answer the big boss gave me as a strange eccentric response, but then I was able to understand what he meant. If we were working on the ceiling, then the ceiling was taken for granted. This is your core job... **of course** you are going to do it well, that is your business. Less than a perfect job on the ceiling was unacceptable. Where you can really make a difference is in the details, the little things. One of those details that seems obvious to me today: **the floor needs to be clean**. When you leave your job site for the day, that floor needs to be clean and presentable. Even if we are coming back tomorrow just to make a mess of that same floor again, just to clean it again at the end of the day. 

Because even though the job site is a work in progress and anyone would understand a bit of a mess, that place has an owner. We are working for a client that likes to see the project coming to life. We are building a house... what would be a home soon. So that wise man saw everything he needed to know about how the work was going by looking at the little details and the stuff that "does not matter", because how you do one thing, you do them all. If that floor is clean, you can be pretty confident that the ceiling will be pristine.

I tried to keep that lesson present in my following jobs, and I still try it today when coding. I clean up after myself, I try to leave things better than I found them, I take care of details, I care for things "that you don't see"... This is one way to strive for excellence. It doesn't mean that I always accomplish it, but I sure aim for it.

# It even works backwards

For the sake of the argument, let's accept with the premise "how you do one thing you do them all". Maybe we can try to make it work backward. Meaning, you can do "right" the little easy tasks and that will be contagious to your way and end up changing the way you do other more difficult tasks.

For example, it is very probable that how you organize your physical desktop is very similar to how you organize your virtual desktop on your computer. At least it is in my home... without entering into details, when you see a desk, if you open the computer on that desk you will see a pretty good virtual replica in terms of tidiness. You can start with the easier task of cleaning up your virtual desktop on your computer, which is way easier than cleaning and organizing your real one. You get the trick... you get accustomed to working with a "tidy virtual desktop" and since how you do one thing, you do them all, you are going to end up working on a real tidy desktop.

The example is a bit of a stretch but I hope I get the point across. What I mean is that the little things matter because you get used to doing things a certain way and that way permeates into other aspects of your life. We can take advantage of that and do really well a bunch of little easy tasks in our day-to-day.

# A couple silly examples

I sing lullabies with my guitar at night to my children at bedtime, even though my vocal skills are doubtful, I really try to hit the notes right, every time. I try to improve my fingering on the guitar; I try to do it a little bit better each time. Do they care about the _quality_ of the songs? Of course they don't, they couldn't care less... but I care. Because I think my children deserve my best. I am not going to win a Grammy award, but I can make their songs enjoyable. I refuse to simply go throuht the motions, treating these moments as mere tasks to be completed in autopilot, hoping for them just to sleep so I can go on with other stuff. Right now I am playing guitar, I am singing, this is what is important, let's do it right.

Same thing when I sit down with them to draw and paint, we do it every Thursday. I am not very skilled at this at all, but I try hard to make something decent. Again, they only care that I am doing crafts with them; the final outcome is not important. But while doing it like this, I am creating the habit of trying my best every time and **habits are very powerful**. Paying attention to these details makes me more present and also makes me enjoy the activity way more.

# Take over

I've come to appreciate the invaluable lessons learned by the journey —the seasoned sage of a boss, the enigmatic yet insightful mentor, the liberating guidance of my father, and the strong group dynamic within the whole gang. These experiences have instilled in me a profound appreciation for meticulousness, attentiveness, and the pursuit of excellence. 

When writing code, I strive for clarity, readability, and maintainability, not just for the sake of technical proficiency but also for nurturing a clear and focused mind. I aspire for my code to transcend mere functionality, to be a testament to diligence and care, comprehensible to both present and future eyes. Embracing this attitude not only improves my coding habilities but also permeates into every facet of my life, enriching my relationships, roles, and character. For as one man once said, how you do one thing, you do them all.
